# Report: is Bostrom's simulation argument hard to vary?

**The question, frozen.** The paper answers several. The title and abstract make the central one: *at least one of (1) fP≈0, (2) fI≈0, (3) fsim≈1 is true.* That is a **derived conclusion** — a disjunction that follows from a count — so I test its conditions by dropping them, not by flipping the outcome. The secondary question, "what should *I* believe about my own case?", is backward ("what can I tell from where I sit"); I keep it separate and mark it, but don't test it here. Range: all human-level civilizations; asked of observers with human-type experiences.

**The explanation in parts.** Bostrom weakens his substrate premise himself and says the argument needs only the weak version; I test that version.

**Part by part**

| Part | Mark | What holds it / what would settle it |
|---|---|---|
| A. Substrate-independence (synaptic-level replication yields experience) | **Fixed** | Put outside the test by the owner and said so ("we shall here take it as a given"). Its real support is **borrowed** from the philosophy of mind, not tested here. |
| B. Posthumans can run vastly many ancestor-simulations cheaply (NI enormous) | **Held** | Remove it and the third horn isn't forced; the disjunction needn't hold. Built from known physics/engineering **lower bounds**, not asserted. |
| B′. The exact figures (10⁴², 10³³⁻³⁶ ops) | **Loose** | Bostrom says being off by orders of magnitude doesn't matter. Near neighbours do the same work. What's held is the *size of the gap*, not the numbers. |
| C. Two cost-per-mind estimates (retina vs synapse count) | **Two routes** | Either estimate carries the argument; neither is needed alone. |
| D. The counting identity fsim = fP·fI·NI/(1+fP·fI·NI) | **Held** | It is the derivation. Drop it and nothing follows. A derived step: test by dropping a condition. |
| E. Bland indifference principle (credence = fsim) | **Held if** | It does the credence job *only if* "we have no information about which group we're in" is real — a disputed condition (the self-sampling/self-indication split). Settle by a case that separates it from the rival. |
| E′. The betting and 98%→99.9999% reassurance | **Loose** | A different reassurance would do as well. |
| F. Reference class: "observers with human-type experiences" | **Held** | Held by the job of answering the title question. Swap to "all observers" and you answer a different question — though its extent is a free stipulation. |
| G. The seamlessness patch (fill in detail, edit or rerun to hide anomalies) | **Held if** | A **catch-all**: it absorbs any internal anomaly, and no gauge is named that would show it swallowing that job. Settle with a stated gauge. |
| H. "Novel physics can't be ruled out" | **Idle** | The argument deliberately uses lower bounds; this widener carries no weight. |
| I. The interest term fI | **Unknown** | Settle by our own trajectory: if we start building ancestor-simulations, the disjunction resolves. |

No totals. One missing load-bearing part can sink a list.

**Whole-explanation checks.**
- **Flip.** Not used on the conclusion: it covers every outcome *because it is derived*, not because it is loose. Tested instead by dropping its one condition, "NI is enormous" (B).
- **Direction.** Section IV is the forward step; Section V is backward. The paper keeps them apart and says which is which. Good.
- **Answer hidden in the starting points?** Not circular — but nearly all the empirical reach sits in the single premise B. Drop B and the disjunction is trivially satisfiable. The logic is hard to vary; the reach is carried by one premise. That is a finding, not a fault.
- **Where the jobs came from.** The paper names its own jobs (make the disjunction follow; locate us among observers) and adds the "implications" job itself. My job — "it should say something about our own near future" — is **added**, so it is *held if* that job is real.
- **Pairs that pull.** The multi-level hierarchy pulls against basement cost: nested simulations need a base simulator that can afford them, which counts against many levels. Finer required simulation pulls against cheap simulation — the line is drawn at synapse-level, and what would show it misplaced is evidence that sub-synaptic detail changes experience other than through synaptic computation.
- **Catch-alls.** G has no gauge (flagged). H is a range-widener but idle here.
- **What the change list leaves out.** It ranges over fP, fI, NI across civilizations and says the time-scale doesn't matter — said up front. It makes no claim about our actions, and takes simulated consciousness as fixed.
- **Rivals.** Bostrom builds the nearest rival (the stronger Doomsday indifference principle) and names the separating change (whether you sample all people even when you know your era). A rival he doesn't build: "we have positive information we're biological."
- **Provenance.** A borrowed, declared given; B built from lower bounds, its figures fitted; C derived; E borrowed from his anthropics work, propped by analogy; I asserted/unknown.

**What would make it harder to vary.** (i) Give the indifference principle a gauge — name one observation that would lower credence in (3), or argue the "no information" condition is real. (ii) Tie the enormous-NI premise to a checkable prediction about our own trajectory.

**What this does not show.** Hard to vary is not true. The disjunction could be false — if substrate-independence fails, or the physics premise is wrong in a way not yet met — and the argument could still be tight. Passing does not certify (3). The loose figures cost nothing.

**One next step.** Run one poke on E: find a change that makes the bland principle and a self-sampling rival give different verdicts. If none exists, record that at this level they are one explanation, and ask whether you need a finer question.
